Figure 4.26 depicts the mooring line arrangement of the CO ship at Berth 2 2 30, ensuring that the ship can be securely moored during CO transfer operations. 2 Page78 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version Figure 4.24: Existing Berth 30 Before Modifications Figure 4.25: Berth 30 After Modifications Page79 of158 T-RICH Pre-FEED Report – Public Version Figure 4.26: CO Ship Mooring Arrangement at Berth 30 2 The allowable ship draft at Berth 30 is another important consideration when evaluating it for compatibility with the CO ship design. The CO ship with a capacity of 20,000 tons of CO is expected to 2 2 2 have a fully-laden draft of less than 30 feet. By comparison, the Tampa Bay Pilots Association states an allowable draft at Berth 30 of 43’-6”16. This allows for an under keel clearance (UKC) of 13’-6” which is substantially more than the typical minimum required 2’-0” UKC. Should expansion of T-RICH ever justify the construction of a second marine berth to accommodate more CO ships which would be required for 2 a greater overall transportation system throughput, such a berth could be constructed at the open shoreline along the north side of the parcel designated as “Berth 29”. The Tampa Bay Pilots Association designates the maximum vessel draft in this area as 34’-07”, still comfortably deeper than the maximum expected draft of the CO ship of less than 30’-0”. 2 The “capacity” of a marine berth is dictated by the number of ships that can be handled there per week, which is primarily limited by the speed at which the ship can be loaded or discharged given the type of cargo transfer that occurs there. With container terminals or bulk aggregate terminals, shoreside cranes will typically be one of the primary limiting factors to how fast the ship can get in and out and vacate the berth for the next ship. But for berths where fluids are transferred, such as liquefied CO , it is primarily 2 the sizes of pumps and piping which dictate how fast the fluid can be transferred on or off the vessel. T- RICH has been designed with ship loading piping and pumps so that the ship can be loaded in less than 18 hours. When the required time is added to that to tie up the vessel, hook up cargo hoses, and make all preparations for the fluid transfer, and the reverse of that process at the conclusion of cargo transfer, the CO ship should have to spend no more than 24 hours at T-RICH’s berth. This means, hypothetically, that 2 Berth 30 could handle up to 7 CO ships per week. Since only 2 ships per week are required to meet the 2 hub’s annual throughput goal of 2 million tons per annum (mtpa), Berth 30 has more than enough capacity to meet that goal and even accommodate future expansion to the hub with associated increases in annual throughput.
